source.provider: NOAA Climate Prediction Center (CPC), distributed by NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory (PSL)
source.index: Oceanic Niño Index (ONI): 3-month running mean of ERSST.v6 sea-surface temperature anomalies, Niño 3.4 region (5°N–5°S, 120°–170°W)
source.note: Each monthly value is the 3-month season centred on that month (January = DJF). Since 2026 CPC ranks El Niño strength with the Relative ONI (RONI), which removes tropical-wide warming and is usually somewhat lower than the traditional ONI used here.

definition.rule: El Niño: ONI ≥ +0.5 °C for at least five consecutive overlapping 3-month seasons; La Niña: ≤ −0.5 °C.
definition.strength_note: Peak-based categories commonly used for the ONI; not an official NOAA classification.

current_status.summary: NOAA reports that El Niño keeps strengthening and that a strong-to-very strong event is likely through January–March 2027 (probability above 83%).

game_2015.note: Only what a player in 2015 could know: ONI seasons ending by December 2015 and the event so far.
game_2015.player_text: 2015: a very strong El Niño is building in the Pacific (Oceanic Niño Index +2.45 °C in OND). The last comparable events, 1982–83 and 1997–98, brought marine heatwaves and droughts across the tropics.

present_alert.player_text: Today: NOAA has an El Niño Advisory in force. The Oceanic Niño Index reached +2.46 °C in ASO 2026, close to the 1997 and 2015 record events, and a strong-to-very strong El Niño is likely through early 2027.

indicators.label: Root-zone soil wetness
indicators.player_text: In El Niño years, root-zone soil wetness here tends to run lower than its trend: about 0.055 on its 0–1 scale per +1 °C of the Oceanic Niño Index (NASA POWER 1981–2014, r = -0.51).
